newsitem.title: USA: ABA panel letter outlines "pay to play" concerns.
newsitem.headline: ABA panel letter outlines "pay to play" concerns.

text.p: A key American Bar Association panel this week continued to voice its strong opposition to a controversial New York City bar proposal on curbing "pay-to-play" by lawyers.
The ABA's influential standing committee on ethics and professional responsibility on Friday released a letter it sent April 23 to heads of all ABA standing committees and sections on the issue.

The letter, signed by panel chairman Lawrence Fox, a partner with Drinker Biddle & Reath in Philadelphia, urges panel members to reject the proposal by the Association of the Bar of the City of New York when ABA delegates meet at ABA's annual meeting in August.
As reported by Reuters on April 21, the ABA ethics panel voted to send the letter at a meeting in Bermuda last weekend.
But Fox's letter does not recommend closing the door on any further action by ABA on the issue.

"It may be that the issue of lawyers making contributions to public officials whose entities hire lawyers for any legal work is one that the ABA should explore further," Fox's three- page letter says.
"This current proposal, however, is badly flawed and inappropriately directed, and we continue to conclude should be firmly rejected," Fox said.

At the center of the debate is a new rule adopted by the City bar that would prohibit muni lawyers that solicit or make contributions to municipal clients, including some PAC contributions, from engaging in bond business for two years with those governments.
The rule is partly modeled after a standard adopted by the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board in 1994 for muni bond dealers, although the City bar's rule is more restrictive.

Fox's letter says the ethics panel opposes the City bar'ss rule because ABA "Model Rules" already "make it unethical to pay a public official a bribe" and prohibit lawyers from giving "anything of value to a person for recommending a lawyer's services."

But Michael Cardozo, president of the New York City bar group, took issue with Fox's letter. "(ABA's) regulation prohibits a bribe. We're not talking about a bribe," Cardozo said "We're not saying that some muni official says I'm going to give this money to the highest bidder."

"What we are (referring to is when) everyone is told to buy the 10 tickets to the political dinner. You pay to have the influence, you pay to get on the list. If you don't, you ain't going to get on my list," Cardozo said.
Fox's letter also says that ABA already has a clear policy calling for full disclosure of contributions.
And if there has been a contribution made, it is the public official seeking the contribution who is guilty of an "ethical breach," not necessarily the lawyer, Fox's letter says.

The letter adds that a lawyer's contribution to a client municipal official is not "per se ... illegal or unethical." Also, ABA should not back a rule that "abridges lawyers' appropriate roles in the political process, leaving the field open to all others," the letter says.

William Josephson, who chaired the City bar panel that studied pay-to-play, said, "I'm sorry that it's taken this long for the ethics committee to take a position on this issue. And I regret very much that position."
Josephson said the City bar officials will respond to the letter at upcoming speaking engagements.

City bar officials say they repeatedly tried to work with ABA officials on the policy before they issued it ealier this year, but were unsuccessful. But Fox and other ABA officials say they never had meaningful input in the policy.

"Mr. Fox is incorrect when he says we have refused to have a dialogue with him," said Michael Cardozo, president of the City bar. "At every opportunity, we asked all interested ABA people, including Mr. Fox, to have a discussion with us."
--Vicky Stamas, 202-898-8314
